description: We are young advanced students from different parts of Argentina combining our carrers into a real-impact solution for this upcoming Hackton. We are interested in create a proposal that reflects a positive impact in the enviroment while using data or satelital images combining our knowledges.
summary:
FIREN’T is a public web app, with an open Python notebook and all code on GitHub, that puts more than twenty years of fire in Argentina on a single scale. NASA FIRMS records fire with two sensors: MODIS since 2003 and VIIRS since 2012, whose smaller pixels detect about 3.4 times more hotspots over the same fires. Stitching the two records together invents a trend: the raw paste says fire rose 129%, when the harmonized record shows 30% less fire in 2012–2025 than in 2003–2011.

We cleaned both records with the same criteria and compared them only on days both sensors observed. We tested four machine learning methods, using region and season as inputs to convert MODIS to the VIIRS scale, and picked the winner with a rule fixed before seeing the test results. We split Argentina into six regions because each burns differently, and since FIRMS is global, the method can be replicated in any country. The result answers CONAE’s challenge: one consistent record from 2003 to October 2026, with early warnings and a seasonal curve for critical periods. The app is built to be accessible to the whole community in every sense: plain words, four languages, options for low vision, color blindness and read-aloud, shareable links and a forum to report odd data. It matters because fire policy, emergency planning and public debate need trends they can trust, readable by specialists and everyone else alike.
details:
Satellite observations are an essential tool for understanding wildfire activity, but different sensors do not detect fires in the same way. VIIRS generally detects more hotspots than MODIS because of its finer spatial resolution, about 3.4 times more over the same fires in Argentina. Combining their records without accounting for these differences can make fire activity appear to increase when the change actually comes from the sensor. Simply pasting both records together suggests that 2012–2025 had 129% more fire than 2003–2011. Once harmonized, the record shows 30% less: the opposite conclusion. FIREN’T addresses this problem in Argentina by turning fragmented observations into one consistent historical record from January 2003 to October 2026.

We downloaded all hotspots for Argentina directly from NASA FIRMS (firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov) as CSV files, combining the final archive with near-real-time data for the latest months, and used CONAE’s hotspot catalog as a reference. We focused on Argentina for three reasons: it is the challenge proposed by CONAE, it is our country, and it is a demanding test. Argentina stretches from 22° to 55° south, from the Chaco forest to the Patagonian woodlands, so the method has to work with very different kinds of fire.

We merge NASA FIRMS data from MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP C2 as the reference sensor, and VIIRS NOAA-20 C2 to fill gaps. All sensors use the same geographical boundaries and cleaning criteria: vegetation fires only, with 230,191 fixed heat sources such as industries and gas flares removed. Extreme events are kept, because they are real. Sensors are compared only on days when both recorded observations, from 2012 to 2025. Of the 62 days without S-NPP data, 59 were filled using NOAA-20 (ratio 1.03, 3.9% error) and the remaining three with MODIS. Every reconstructed day is flagged.

We split the country into five regions with their own fire regimes, chosen for their number of hotspots or the impact of their fires, plus a sixth zone for the rest of the country:

  • Gran Chaco (land clearing)
  • Paraná Delta (wetland burning)
  • Sierras de Córdoba (dry-season wildfires)
  • Corrientes and Iberá (marshes)
  • Andean Patagonia (forests)

This matters because each sensor “sees” differently depending on the type of fire. The VIIRS/MODIS ratio ranges from 3.10 in the Gran Chaco to 4.74 in the Paraná Delta, so a single national factor (3.39) would introduce bias in every region.

We framed the conversion of MODIS to the VIIRS scale as a machine learning problem, using region and season as inputs, and compared four methods: fixed factor, logarithmic regression, quantile mapping and Random Forest. We trained on 2012–2021 and tested on unseen observations from 2022–2025. Before evaluating the results, we established the selection criteria:

  • error within 5% of the best-performing model
  • bias below 10%
  • worst-year error below 25%
  • model simplicity as the tie-breaker

The best method was selected separately for each indicator. Logarithmic regression was selected for hotspots (bias −3.5%, worst-year error 13.5%) and for fire radiative power (bias −1.4%), while quantile mapping performed best for fire-days (bias +1.5%). Random Forest did not justify its complexity. We also report 95% confidence intervals from a block bootstrap.

As final checks, we verified that the harmonization does not introduce an artificial discontinuity in 2012, and that our three indicators (hotspots, fire-days and fire radiative power) agree strongly, with correlations from 0.92 to 0.98. All three flag the same extreme years: 2020, 2003 and 2008.

The application compares harmonized hotspot activity over the last 7, 15 or 30 days of data with the same calendar window in each historical reference year. Activity above the 75th percentile is classified as elevated, and activity above the 90th percentile as exceptional.

A cumulative seasonal curve places the current year against historical reference levels: the median, the 10th–90th percentile range and the record season. This shows whether the current fire season is running ahead of or behind the usual pace.

These tools let anyone see whether fire activity is usual, elevated or exceptional without needing a scientific background. Featured cases include the Paraná Delta in 2020 (+1,176%), Sierras de Córdoba in 2020 (+586%) and Corrientes in 2022 (+150%), compared with their historical reference levels.

Researchers get an open notebook, confidence intervals, flagged reconstructed days and a custom area analysis tool. Other users can explore interactive maps (including the Islas Malvinas) and historical calendars, download data as CSV files, share links that reproduce the exact same view, and leave comments that the team reviews, answers and publishes.

FIREN’T is more than a wildfire map. It combines scientific rigor, historical context and accessibility in one platform, designed to be useful to researchers, citizens, educators and environmental organizations alike.

The application is available in Spanish, English, Portuguese and a Guaraní prototype. On arrival, it asks each person about their needs. It offers large, high-contrast text with a magnifier that turns on with the low-vision option, colorblind-friendly visualizations, and read-aloud summaries.

Because NASA FIRMS provides global satellite observations, the methodology can be adapted to other countries by editing a bounding box and the region file and re-running the notebook. That makes FIREN’T a potentially scalable approach to understanding wildfire activity.

These are future directions, not features of the current version:

  • real-time alerts through SMS, push notifications or WhatsApp when hotspots are detected near a user’s location
  • fire-spread scenarios combining satellite observations with soil moisture, topography, vegetation and wind
  • risk maps for communities and critical infrastructure such as roads, schools, hospitals and electrical substations
  • post-fire assessments to support restoration and reforestation

Each of these would require additional datasets, dedicated models, and validation against real wildfire events.

We used Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic, to support code development and writing. The team made all methodological decisions and reviewed and verified every numerical result. The used tools are Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and PyArrow), Jupyter notebooks in Google Colab, Streamlit, Plotly, Folium and GitHub, with NASA FIRMS data complemented by CONAE resources.

Throughout development, we took into account differences between satellite sensors, missing observation days and regional fire regimes, so that data gaps would not be mistaken for periods of low fire activity.

We also accounted for the highly skewed distribution of wildfire data, which is why we use percentiles instead of z-scores. To avoid overfitting, we tested our models on unseen years and set the evaluation criteria in advance. We are also open about our limits: the Terra and Aqua satellites, which carry MODIS, are aging, and the most recent months are provisional near-real-time data.

 

Transparency, reproducibility and accessibility were equally important throughout the process. Our goal was to build a tool that not only produces reliable scientific results but also makes them understandable and useful to different audiences.
